title: SERVING GOD CAN BECOME A DISTRACTION FROM GOD
paragraphs: SERVING GOD CAN BECOME A DISTRACTION FROM GOD
Some of the people furthest from God's heart are standing closest to His work.
It sounds like something that should not be true.
Yet Scripture repeatedly reveals a terrifying reality: it is possible to spend your life doing things for God while slowly drifting away from God Himself.
You can preach and stop praying.
Build a kingdom in His name while neglecting the King.
The danger is not always rebellion.
Sometimes the danger is religious activity.
Sometimes the greatest threat to intimacy with God is not sin.
It is distraction disguised as service.
The tragedy is that many believers do not realize it is happening until their souls are exhausted, their hearts are empty, and their relationship with Christ feels strangely distant.
But somewhere along the journey, they lost the wonder of simply being with Him.
One of the most powerful examples appears in Luke 10.
Jesus enters a home where two sisters respond very differently to His presence.
The story feels familiar because most of us have been Martha.
The Greek word Luke uses is "περιεσπᾶτο" (periespato).
It literally means to be pulled away, dragged in different directions, distracted from what matters most.
Martha was not distracted by sin.
She was preparing food for Jesus.
Yet her service pulled her away from Jesus.
The work that began as devotion had become agitation.
"Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary."
The issue was never the serving.
The issue was that serving had displaced sitting.
The church in Ephesus looked extraordinarily successful.
"I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first."
The terrifying reality is that Jesus praised their work before confronting their heart.
The church had not abandoned ministry.
Many believers today know how to work for God.
Far fewer know how to rest in God.
Far fewer know how to abide.
Many know how to serve Christ.
Far fewer know how to simply love Him.
The applause of ministry can become louder than the voice of God.
And when that happens, spiritual success becomes spiritual danger.
One of the most devastating examples appears in Luke 15.
Far fewer notice the older brother.
The younger brother ran away from the father.
Yet when the father celebrated the younger son's return, the older brother's heart was exposed.
"These many years I have served you."
It means to labor as a slave.
The older brother did not see himself as a beloved son.
He saw himself as an employee.
He had spent years near the father without truly enjoying the father.
Many Christians secretly live this way.
They are exhausted because they are trying to earn what God freely gives.
They serve from obligation rather than affection.
They work from fear rather than love.
They labor for approval instead of from approval.
The result is burnout, bitterness, and spiritual emptiness.
Because sons and daughters thrive in relationship.
Jesus Never Called Us to Produce Fruit
That statement sounds shocking until you finish the sentence.
Jesus never called us to produce fruit.
In John 15, Jesus repeatedly uses the Greek word "μένω" (menō).
Fruit is the natural outcome of connection.
A branch does not strain to create grapes.
It remains attached to the vine.
The life of the vine produces what the branch never could.
Many believers are exhausted because they are trying to manufacture what only abiding can produce.
More effort will not solve a disconnected soul.
More ministry will not heal spiritual dryness.
More activity will not create intimacy.
The answer is not doing more for Jesus.
The answer is returning to Jesus.
The Hidden Idol of Christian Productivity
Modern Christianity often rewards visible activity.
None of these are inherently wrong.
But they become dangerous when they replace communion with Christ.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly reveal God's concern with the heart.
"Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart."
The Hebrew word for heart is "לֵבָב" (levav).
It refers to the inner person.
God has always been after hearts before accomplishments.
The Kingdom of God has never been advanced primarily by busy people.
It has been advanced by surrendered people.
The greatest saints in history were not known first for what they did.
They were known for who they walked with.
Before David was king, he was a worshiper.
Before Peter was a preacher, he was a disciple.
Before Paul was an apostle, he was a man captured by Christ.
Then imagine Him asking one question.
Not how much did you build.
Not how much did you accomplish.
Not how many followers you gained.
Not how much influence you accumulated.
The greatest reward of Christianity has never been heaven.
The greatest reward has always been Christ Himself.
The Gospel is not merely forgiveness.
The cross was not only designed to remove sin.
It was designed to remove every barrier between us and Him.
Maybe this article exposed something uncomfortable.
Maybe your spiritual life feels more professional than personal.
Maybe your service has become heavier than your worship.
Maybe your ministry has become louder than your prayer life.
Maybe your schedule has become fuller while your soul has become emptier.
Then hear the invitation of Jesus.
Worship without needing anything from Him again.
Because one day every sermon will end.
Every ministry position will pass away.
But Jesus Christ will remain forever.
And in the end, the greatest treasure was never what you did for Him.
It was that you walked with Him.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
One day you will discover that the thing you thought you were giving to God was the very thing keeping you from sitting beside Him.
